# Selection — TRD §15 row 1: the concrete algorithm suite and crypto-agility

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-18
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 1 · **Scope of:** review 3a (storage and journal)
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.2, §13.10, §6.1, §10.9 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.1
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json`](../../test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-suite-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-suite-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 2](./row-2-journal-aead.md) selected the synchronous half of this suite;
[row 3](./row-3-record-format.md) selects the formats built out of it.

---

## The selection

```
Suite 1

  Content store AEAD         AES-256-GCM                       WebCrypto           async
  Local key envelope AEAD    AES-256-GCM                       WebCrypto           async
  Network envelope AEAD      AES-256-GCM                       WebCrypto           async
  Synchronous journal AEAD   XChaCha20-Poly1305                wasm/journal-seal   sync   [row 2]
                             audited RustCrypto chacha20poly1305, compiled to an
                             inlined wasm module, instantiated synchronously
  Subkey derivation          HKDF-SHA-256                      WebCrypto           async
  Mutation signatures        Ed25519                           WebCrypto           async
  Public-key wrap            HPKE base mode (RFC 9180)
                             DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM
                             = 0x0020 / 0x0001 / 0x0002
  Hash                       SHA-256                           WebCrypto

Agility    A carrier version selects the entire suite. There is no per-record
           algorithm identifier, no negotiation, and therefore nothing to
           downgrade. Domain labels are done/<carrier>/v<suite>. Every carrier
           authenticates its own version in its associated data.

Reader     A fixed compiled-in set of (carrier, version) pairs. Accept exactly
           those; refuse everything else, including versions above your own.
           Refusal is reported and leaves the carrier intact.

Deferred   Nothing. Rows 4, 12, 13 and 14 have taken every role this row
           deferred, and their answers are in the suite above.
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. Half of this row was decided by row 2, and neither row noticed at the time

TRD §13.2 forbids one primitive **key** crossing the asynchronous/synchronous boundary. TRD §13.10 states the
criterion more strongly, as no **primitive** shared between the two paths. Row 2 then took
XChaCha20-Poly1305 for the journal — which, under the stronger reading, removes the ChaCha family from every
asynchronous role in the system.

**What remains is not a shortlist.** The requirement for the asynchronous paths is an AEAD that is native, so
it costs no bundle on the cold-start path §12 already flags as the budget at risk, and reviewed, so review 3a
is reading a primitive rather than a preference. **WebCrypto offers exactly one AEAD, and it is AES-GCM** —
`encrypt`/`decrypt` support RSA-OAEP, AES-CTR, AES-CBC and AES-GCM, and only the last authenticates. So once
row 2 spent the sync slot on ChaCha, the async slot was decided by the platform.

That is worth saying plainly rather than presenting the outcome as a judgment. **The suite's largest choice
fell out of a decision taken for unrelated reasons**, and this row's job on that half is to write it down,
check it, and notice that the constraint did real work — §13.2 is satisfied here by construction rather than
incidentally, which is the property the review should be told about.

**The open half is agility**, and it was open in a way that was easy to miss: three version markers already
exist in the codebase and the plan, invented separately and meaning different things. §4 is about that.

---

## 2. The suite, role by role

| Role                     | Selected                                                                   | Why this one                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Content store AEAD       | AES-256-GCM, WebCrypto                                                     | The only AEAD the platform supplies; hardware-accelerated on every target; no bundle                                   |
| Local key envelope AEAD  | AES-256-GCM, WebCrypto                                                     | Same path, and `L_local` is already an AES-GCM `CryptoKey` under §13.3                                                 |
| Network envelope AEAD    | AES-256-GCM, WebCrypto                                                     | Named so the suite is complete; its **wire format** is row 4 and review 3b                                             |
| Synchronous journal AEAD | XChaCha20-Poly1305, RustCrypto crate as inlined wasm (`wasm/journal-seal`) | [Row 2](./row-2-journal-aead.md). The only primitive the platform does not supply, and the only one on the crash path  |
| Subkey derivation        | HKDF-SHA-256, WebCrypto `deriveBits`                                       | Derivation is once-per-open, where async is free. The labels are what make §13.2's separation real rather than nominal |
| Mutation signatures      | Ed25519, WebCrypto                                                         | Small, fast, widely reviewed. §7 records what still has to be confirmed about availability                             |
| Public-key wrap          | HPKE base mode, X25519 / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM                         | RFC 9180's most widely implemented ciphersuite; covers the `R_pub` and per-reader wrap cases uniformly (§13.2)         |
| Hash                     | SHA-256                                                                    | One hash wherever HKDF, signatures and commitments need one                                                            |

**Three roles are named here but used only past this review**, and naming them is the point: the envelope
AEAD, signatures and HPKE all belong to review 3b's rows, and leaving their primitives unnamed until then
would mean the separation rule in §3 could only be checked over half the system.

**The synchronous role adds no runtime dependency at all, and `@noble/ciphers` stays a `devDependency`.** An
earlier draft of this row had it shipping, and said Stage 1 would move it to `dependencies`. Row 2 then measured
the pure-JS library over the §12 budget and replaced it with the compiled seal (row 2 §7), so what ships is an
inlined wasm module and nothing is moved. **`@noble` kept a job, and it is a better one:** it is the independent
implementation the journal vectors are generated from, which is what makes `scripts/check-wasm-seal.mjs` a
cross-implementation check rather than the shipped module agreeing with itself.

**One role is named without a test vector, deliberately.** HPKE has published vectors in RFC 9180 §A, but
Node's WebCrypto has no HPKE and no library is selected, so a vector here would be transcribed rather than
verified — and a transcribed vector in a self-verifying file is exactly the thing §9 exists to prevent. The
ciphersuite identifiers are pinned; the vector arrives in review 3b's scope with the implementation that can
check it.

---

## 3. The separation rule, made executable

The two statements of the rule are not the same sentence:

> §13.2 — "One primitive **key** must not be reused across the asynchronous and synchronous constructions."
>
> §13.10 — "no **primitive** reused across the asynchronous and synchronous paths."

The second is strictly stronger, and the suite satisfies it — intersection empty:

| Path             | Primitives                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **asynchronous** | AES-256-GCM · ES256 (ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256) · Ed25519 · HKDF-SHA-256 · HPKE base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM · SHA-256 |
| **synchronous**  | XChaCha20-Poly1305                                                                                                                                                      |

**This was a sentence listing four primitives, and the suite had grown to six** (`S0-1`). ES256 arrived with row
12 and HPKE with row 10's wraps; neither edit came back here, so the set this row published as the separation
argument had not been true for some time. It is a table now because a table is what the generator can read — the
sets are compared against `SUITE_1` in both directions on every `pnpm check`, so the next role added fails here
rather than quietly narrowing the claim.

**The generator asserts that intersection rather than this document claiming it.** `checkSeparation()`
classifies every role by path and fails the build if any primitive appears on both. A later edit that satisfies
only the weaker reading — same primitive, different keys — fails there instead of being caught by a reviewer, or
not caught. That is the whole reason the suite is data in a script rather than a table in prose.

**Which of the two is enforced was never decided until now, and it is not decided on strength**
([`S0-1`](../review/remediation/S0-1/README.md)). The stronger reading wins because **a suite names primitives
and does not name keys**: _no primitive key reused_ cannot be asserted from this data at all — it needs a
derivation graph — so selecting it would mean an oracle enforcing nothing while this row says it does. §13.2's
rule follows from §13.10's, one rule is enforced, and nothing in the suite violates it.

**`path` says where a primitive _executes_, and the column has three values.** `async`, `sync`, and `none` for a
role selecting no primitive at all. HKDF-SHA-256 derives the journal subkey — a key used synchronously — and is
`async` because the derivation runs at open. Stating that is not pedantry: _it produces something the sync path
uses_ is a live reading, and it is how a fourth value gets added.

**And the check was passing on a fourth value the whole time** (`f-3bea0e6-suite-separation-ignores-both-path`).
`checkSeparation()` selected each bucket by matching a label, so a role matching neither entered neither — and a
role in neither bucket cannot be in their intersection. `hash` was labelled `both`, so **the set listed above was
this document's claim and not the generator's**, for the entire life of a check written to stop exactly that.
Nothing on the synchronous path hashes, so `hash` is `async` and the two agree now. `both` is refused with the
rule it violates rather than as an unknown value, an unrecognised label is refused because **a classification
that drops what it does not recognise can only pass**, and a `none` role naming a real primitive is refused
before `none` becomes the next hatch.

Two smaller invariants are checked the same way: every carrier maps to a defined suite and authenticates its
own version, and every role is either selected or deferred to a **named row**, so nothing falls through the
gap between the two lists.

**Naming a row turned out not to be enough, and §7 records what that cost.** The check read the owner string,
which stays true-looking forever; it now reads TRD §15.1 and fails if a deferred role points at a row that has
since been selected.

---

## 4. Agility: versioned suites, not negotiated algorithms

This is the half of row 1 that was genuinely open, and the shape of the answer matters more than the answer.

**The rule.** A carrier's version field selects an **entire suite**. There is no algorithm identifier in any
record. A reader knows a fixed, compiled-in set of `(carrier, version)` pairs, accepts exactly those, and
refuses everything else.

**Why not the obvious thing.** The obvious design is an algorithm field per record — a cipher identifier, or a
small negotiation. It is rejected, and not on size grounds. **A negotiable algorithm field is what makes a
downgrade attack possible at all.** §15 row 15 already requires interrupted rotation and downgrade to "fail
closed without changing the confidentiality promise". The cheapest way to hold that property is to have no
negotiation surface: there is no field to set, so there is no weaker suite to select.

**And the version is authenticated, so it cannot be edited into one.** Every carrier puts its own version
inside its AAD (row 2 already does; row 3 does for both its formats). A record renumbered from suite 1 to some
other suite fails to open, because the AAD no longer matches what it was sealed under. **That is fail-closed
by construction rather than by a check somebody remembered to write** — and it matters specifically because
these are structured-clone records whose version field is an ordinary editable property to anyone holding the
profile.

**Refusal is reported, never silent.** A carrier the reader cannot accept is left intact and surfaced. This
inherits row 2's rule for the journal — silent deletion is the wrong failure mode for a write-ahead log — and
generalizes it: a read path that discards what it does not understand converts an upgrade mistake into data
loss. Removal stays an explicit repair action.

**Versions above your own are refused too, and that is not conservatism.** A store written by a newer build
means a newer writer touched this profile. Guessing at its framing is how a store gets corrupted; refusing and
saying so is how a user gets told to update.

---

## 5. Two version axes exist, and row 2 already has both

A reader who opens row 2's construction sees `"2:"` as the record prefix and `done/jrnl/v1` as the label, in
the same record, and is entitled to ask which is the version. **Both are, of different things**, and this row
is where that gets named rather than left as an accident:

| Axis                | What it selects                          | Where it lives                                     |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Carrier version** | How to split the bytes — the framing     | The leading integer: `"2:"`, `StoredRecord.v`      |
| **Suite version**   | Which algorithms — this document's table | The trailing integer of the domain label: `.../v1` |

The journal's carrier is at 2 while its suite is at 1 because the carrier counted from 1 when the journal was
**plaintext**: `1:` → `2:` was a framing change, from "base64 of a Yjs update" to "base64 of a sealed record",
and no suite existed on either side of it. So the numbers legitimately differ, and pretending otherwise would
mean renumbering an already-generated vector file to make a cosmetic point.

**What is required is not that the two agree, but that the mapping is total and pinned.** The registry in the
vector file is that mapping, and the generator refuses to emit a carrier that names an undefined suite or a
label whose trailing version disagrees with the suite it claims. Today every carrier maps to suite 1.

**One consequence to state.** Because a carrier version selects a suite wholesale, a suite change bumps every
carrier that uses the changed primitive, even where the framing is byte-identical. That is more version churn
than a per-record algorithm field would produce, and it is the price of not having a negotiation surface. It
is worth paying at this scale, where the carriers number four.

---

## 6. What a suite change costs, per carrier

Worth working out now, because "we can change it later" is the claim agility is supposed to support, and it is
only true where a migration path exists.

| Carrier            | Migration                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Content record     | **The trim already is the migration.** §6.1's trim writes one `state` record under the current generation, waits for its transaction to complete, then deletes what it supersedes. Doing that under a new suite converts the store with no new state machine, and it is already crash-safe in that order |
| Journal entry      | Nothing to migrate. The journal holds only what has not flushed through a 250 ms window; old-suite entries are refused and reported, bounded by that window on one upgrade                                                                                                                               |
| Local key envelope | Re-sealed at the next unlock, while `K_g` is briefly plaintext — the same interval §13.3 already uses for reader and `R_pub` wraps                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Network envelope   | Review 3b. Named here so the gap is visible rather than assumed closed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**That the content store's suite migration is a path that already exists, for other reasons, is the strongest
practical argument for this agility design** and is the thing to put in front of the reviewer. The expensive
part of a crypto migration is normally the in-place conversion state machine; here §6.1 built one for
compaction and it happens to be exactly the right shape.

---

## 7. What is still open, and what this row owes

~~**Ed25519's availability is asserted, not verified.**~~ **Closed on 2026-08-19**, in TRD §10.11. The gap
this row recorded was that the project had **no written browser support matrix** — `docs/development.md` named a
Playwright profile, not a floor — so the availability claim had nothing to check against, and §13.10 anticipated
"a fallback path needed where unavailable" without this row selecting one.

**The floor is Baseline _newly available_, and Ed25519 clears it**: Chrome and Edge 137, Firefox 129, Safari 17.0
on desktop and iOS, with Chrome and Edge the binding constraint. Under that floor there is no unavailable state,
so the fallback path §13.10 anticipated is not a thing to select.

**What closing it turned up is worth more than the answer.** Baseline has one feature for `web-cryptography`,
widely available since 2015 — a decade before Ed25519 was in it — and none per algorithm. So the floor rule this
row wanted written down **cannot resolve this row's own question**, and TRD §10.11 states per-capability floors
separately for exactly that reason. **Half of this row's owed item survives**: the support floor is written, and
the primitive is still not tested against it. Signatures are first used in Stage 4 and the conformance test
belongs there (§11.2).

**HPKE has no vector here**, for the reason in §2. It is pinned by ciphersuite identifier and lands with 3b.

~~**Four roles are deferred to named rows.**~~ **Closed on 2026-08-20, and it closed badly before it closed
well.** All four rows were answered — 4, 12, 13 and 14 — and **this file went on publishing three of the roles as
unfilled**, because the coverage check asserted only that a deferral named a row, never that the row was still
open. A reviewer reading `algorithm-suite.json` in the week of the 24th would have found the slot verifier
described as _assigned to review 3b, not this row's to take_ by a document that row 12 had already answered.

**It is the same drift as the journal provider name, in the same file**, and finding it twice is what makes the
shape worth naming: **a fact about another document, copied here, with nothing checking the copy.** The
provider name was one; the deferral list was three. So the fix is not another correction — `checkCoverage`
now reads §15.1 out of the TRD and fails the build if any deferred role's owning row appears in the selected
half. The two roles §13.10 carries and this file lacked, both answering _none_, are now in the suite:
credential stretching (rows 13 and 14) and slot-verifier stretching (row 12).

**The `devDependency` move is no longer owed**, per §2. Row 2's compiled seal is what ships, so nothing moves
to `dependencies` and Stage 1 inherits nothing here.

**One of this row's own criteria is not obviously satisfied by the journal role, and it is review 3a's to answer.**
The criteria are _reviewed and widely implemented_, _available without a polyfill where possible_, and §13.2
separation. The RustCrypto `chacha20poly1305` crate satisfies the first; what it does not settle is whether
compiling that reviewed source through `rustc` and `wasm32-unknown-unknown` inherits the property, since **the
artifact a user runs is not the artifact anyone reviewed**. TRD §13.10 records this as the only item in 3a's
scope that is a criterion rather than a construction, which is why it sits in this row rather than row 2. What
the project can do about it, it has done: the module is built from a pinned crate, regenerated reproducibly by
`node scripts/build-wasm-seal.mjs`, and checked on every `pnpm check` against draft-irtf-cfrg-xchacha-03 §A.3.1
and row 2's composition vectors — so a compiled artifact that computes something other than XChaCha20-Poly1305
fails the build rather than shipping.

**Nothing in this row is measured.** Row 2 carried bundle and latency figures because it was adding a
dependency to a budgeted path. This row adds no code — AES-GCM, HKDF, Ed25519 and SHA-256 are all platform —
so its only cost is the one already counted against row 2. **The cold-start effect of per-record decryption is
real but belongs to row 3**, which is where the record count enters.

---

## 8. What this row does not decide

Rows 12, 13 and 14 each own a construction that would otherwise look like it belongs in a suite table, and
each is listed in the vector file with its owning row so the omission reads as a decision:

- **Recovery-code stretching (row 14).** §13.10 is right that this is a choice about the code's entropy and
  presentation, not about the KDF. Argon2id-or-none falls out of that, and the presentation is not designed.
- **Slot verifier (row 12).** §15 assigns row 12 to review **3b**, so it is not this row's to take even though
  §13.9's verifier is device-local. That assignment is worth a second look — a local verifier that resists
  offline guessing by a profile holder is storage-shaped, and 3a is the review that will have the context —
  but reassigning a row is a change to §15, not something a selection document should do silently.
- **Device-lock derivation (row 13).** Row 3 defines the key-envelope **format**; row 13 decides what key
  opens it once a device lock is enabled. Naming that seam is how it avoids being designed twice.

---

## 9. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-suite-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check` now
runs it. **The generator verifies itself on every run**, in four ways: every primitive KAT is executed against
WebCrypto, the §13.2/§13.10 separation is asserted over the suite, every carrier is checked against the
registry, and every role is checked to be selected or deferred to a named row **whose §15 entry is still
open** — read out of the TRD rather than trusted to the owner string (§7).

**The KATs are copied, never generated.** AES-256-GCM is Test Case 16 from McGrew and Viega's GCM paper;
HKDF-SHA-256 is RFC 5869 Appendix A Test Case 1; Ed25519 is RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 1; SHA-256 is FIPS 180-4's
one-block `"abc"`. All four reproduce exactly under Node 26's WebCrypto. A KAT produced by the code it checks
proves only that the code agrees with itself, which is why these arrive from outside.

**What the file carries beyond the KATs is the registry itself** — suite 1's roles, the four carriers, and the
acceptance table saying what a reader does with each version it might meet, including the ones it must refuse.
That table is the agility rule in a form an implementation can be driven from, which is the difference between
this row being closed and being described.

**A gap this row closed on the way past.** Row 2's vectors were generated in the previous commit and nothing
ran `--check` on them — not `pnpm check`, not CI. All three vector files are now checked together via
`pnpm vectors:check`, wired into `pnpm check`. A stale vector file is a specification that has quietly stopped
matching its own generator, and it fails silently by construction.
